GOOD NEIGHBOR FENCE ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Morgan Casey

PURPOSE AND PARTIES: THE GOOD NEIGHBOR FENCE ACT
Jordan Lee, the owner of the real property located at 123 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701 ("Party One"), and Morgan Casey, the owner of the real property located at 125 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701 ("Party Two"), are owners of adjoining parcels of real property in California. This document concerns the fence described as: Wood fence along the rear property line.

This document describes California Civil Code Section 841, commonly referred to as the Good Neighbor Fence Act, which addresses the sharing of responsibility between adjoining landowners for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of a boundary fence, and the written notice procedure that statute sets out for a landowner who intends to incur those costs and share them with an adjoining landowner. This document states facts about that statute; it does not tell Party One or Party Two what to do about any specific fence, cost, or disagreement between them. Completing the notice section of this document does not, by itself, guarantee that the notice satisfies every requirement of Section 841 in every circumstance; it is a tool for organizing the content that statute's own text requires a notice to include, described in the following sections.

THE STATUTORY PRESUMPTION OF EQUAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR FENCE COSTS
California's Civil Code states that adjoining landowners share equally in the responsibility for maintaining the boundaries and monuments between their properties. For a fence specifically, the statute states a further, related presumption: adjoining landowners are presumed to share an equal benefit from any fence dividing their properties, and, unless otherwise agreed to by the parties in a written agreement, are presumed to be equally responsible for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence. This presumption applies by its own terms, without requiring the adjoining landowners to first enter into any agreement; it can be displaced only by the landowners' own written agreement stating otherwise, or by rebutting it in the manner described elsewhere in this document. The statute is commonly referred to as the Good Neighbor Fence Act, referencing the bill that enacted its current text, effective January 1, 2014; that popular name does not itself appear in the statute's own text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Adjoining landowners shall share equally in the responsibility for maintaining the boundaries and monuments between them."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 841(a), California Civil Code, adjoining landowners' equal responsibility for maintaining boundaries and monuments (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=841.)
  "Adjoining landowners are presumed to share an equal benefit from any fence dividing their properties and, unless otherwise agreed to by the parties in a written agreement, shall be presumed to be equally responsible for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 841(b)(1), California Civil Code, presumption of equal benefit and equal responsibility for reasonable fence costs, treated as one source with § 841(a) above, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=841.)
  Known gap: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(a) and § 841(b)(1) are both subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code Section 841, and are treated here as two citations from one source, not as independent sources, not independent of one another. Section 841's own text defines "landowner" and "adjoining" (quoted in a companion clause of this document) but does not itself define the word "fence," and the phrase "good neighbor fence" does not appear anywhere in the fetched statutory text of Section 841. This document, like common secondary usage, refers to Section 841 as the "Good Neighbor Fence Act"; that popular name was not independently verified against a specific secondary source in this research session and does not appear in the statute's own fetched text, though the statute's own legislative-history line does confirm its current text was "Repealed and added by Stats. 2013, Ch. 86, Sec. 3. (AB 1404) Effective January 1, 2014." This clause does not evaluate whether the presumption in fact applies, or has been displaced by a written agreement, on the facts of any specific fence or dispute.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF THE 30-DAY PRE-CONSTRUCTION NOTICE
Where a landowner intends to incur costs for a fence subject to the presumption described elsewhere in this document, California's Civil Code requires that landowner to give 30 days' prior written notice to each affected adjoining landowner before incurring those costs. The statute specifies what that notice must include: notification of the presumption of equal responsibility for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence; a description of the nature of the problem facing the shared fence; the proposed solution for addressing the problem; the estimated construction or maintenance costs involved in addressing the problem; the proposed cost-sharing approach; and the proposed timeline for getting the problem addressed. The statute states these as required content of the notice itself; it does not separately prescribe a particular method of delivery (such as personal service or mail) for giving that notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Where a landowner intends to incur costs for a fence described in paragraph (1), the landowner shall give 30 days’ prior written notice to each affected adjoining landowner. The notice shall include notification of the presumption of equal responsibility for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence. The notice shall include a description of the nature of the problem facing the shared fence, the proposed solution for addressing the problem, the estimated construction or maintenance costs involved to address the problem, the proposed cost sharing approach, and the proposed timeline for getting the problem addressed."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 841(b)(2), California Civil Code, 30-day prior written notice and its required content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=841.)
  Known gap: This clause's closing sentence, that the statute does not separately prescribe a particular method of delivery for the notice, describes the absence of such text in Section 841(b)(2) as fetched and reviewed in full; it is not a citation to a specific provision, since there is no text to quote for an absence. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific written notice in fact satisfies Section 841(b)(2)'s content requirements on the facts of a specific fence dispute.

REBUTTING THE PRESUMPTION: STATUTORY FACTORS A COURT MAY CONSIDER
The presumption of equal responsibility described elsewhere in this document is not absolute. California's Civil Code states that the presumption may be overcome by a preponderance of the evidence demonstrating that imposing equal responsibility for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence would be unjust. In determining whether equal responsibility would be unjust, the statute directs a court to consider all of the following: whether the financial burden to one landowner is substantially disproportionate to the benefit conferred upon that landowner by the fence in question; whether the cost of the fence would exceed the difference in the value of the real property before and after its installation; whether the financial burden to one landowner would impose an undue financial hardship given that party's financial circumstances, as demonstrated by reasonable proof; the reasonableness of the particular construction or maintenance project, including the extent to which its costs appear unnecessary or excessive, and the extent to which its costs appear to be the result of a landowner's personal aesthetic, architectural, or other preferences; and any other equitable factors appropriate under the circumstances. This clause lists the statute's own factors; it does not evaluate whether any of them would in fact be found to apply, or would in fact overcome the presumption, on the facts of a specific fence dispute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "The presumption in paragraph (1) may be overcome by a preponderance of the evidence demonstrating that imposing equal responsibility for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence would be unjust. In determining whether equal responsibility for the reasonable costs would be unjust, the court shall consider all of the following: (A) Whether the financial burden to one landowner is substantially disproportionate to the benefit conferred upon that landowner by the fence in question. (B) Whether the cost of the fence would exceed the difference in the value of the real property before and after its installation. (C) Whether the financial burden to one landowner would impose an undue financial hardship given that party’s financial circumstances as demonstrated by reasonable proof. (D) The reasonableness of a particular construction or maintenance project, including all of the following: (i) The extent to which the costs of the project appear to be unnecessary or excessive. (ii) The extent to which the costs of the project appear to be the result of the landowner’s personal aesthetic, architectural, or other preferences. (E) Any other equitable factors appropriate under the circumstances."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 841(b)(3), California Civil Code, standard and factors for overcoming the equal-responsibility presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=841.)
  Known gap: This clause does not evaluate whether any of the listed factors would in fact apply to, or overcome the presumption on, the facts of a specific fence dispute; that determination is committed by the statute's own text to a court applying a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard to the facts before it, not to any generalized fact stated in this document.

WHAT THE STATUTE PROVIDES, AND DOES NOT PROVIDE, IF THE LANDOWNERS DISAGREE
California's Civil Code addresses what happens once a party rebuts the presumption of equal responsibility: where a party rebuts the presumption by a preponderance of the evidence, the statute directs the court, in its discretion and consistent with that party's circumstances, to order either a contribution of less than an equal share of the costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence, or to order no contribution. This is the only outcome Section 841's own text specifies for a disagreement over the presumption. The statute's text, as fetched and reviewed in full for this document, does not itself state what happens if an adjoining landowner simply does not respond to a 30-day notice, does not itself specify a particular court (such as small claims court or superior court) in which a dispute is to be brought, and does not itself describe any required mediation, arbitration, or other pre-litigation step. This is a civil, private-dispute statute concerning cost-sharing between adjoining landowners; its own text does not state that a failure to give notice, to respond to notice, or to share costs as the statute presumes, is a crime or a basis for code enforcement action.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Where a party rebuts the presumption in paragraph (1) by a preponderance of the evidence, the court shall, in its discretion, consistent with the party’s circumstances, order either a contribution of less than an equal share for the costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence, or order no contribution."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 841(b)(4), California Civil Code, court's discretionary order when the presumption is rebutted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=841.)
  Known gap: This clause's statements about what Section 841's text does not address (a non-responding landowner, a specific court such as small claims or superior court, or a required pre-litigation step) describe the absence of such text in the statute as fetched and reviewed in full; they are not citations to specific provisions, since there is no text to quote for an absence, and they should not be read as a claim that no such recourse in fact exists under other statutes (for example, California's small claims court has its own general jurisdictional statutes, which were not researched or cited in this clause) — only that Section 841 itself does not specify one. This clause does not evaluate what remedy, if any, would in fact be available on the facts of a specific dispute.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: "LANDOWNER" AND "ADJOINING"
For purposes of the presumption, notice, and rebuttal framework described elsewhere in this document, California's Civil Code defines two terms. "Landowner" means a private person or entity that lawfully holds any possessory interest in real property, and does not include a city, county, city and county, district, public corporation, or other political subdivision, public body, or public agency — so a public entity that owns adjoining land is not itself a "landowner" for purposes of this presumption. "Adjoining" means contiguous to or in contact with. The statute does not define the word "fence" itself, and does not use the phrase "good neighbor fence" anywhere in its own text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "“Landowner” means a private person or entity that lawfully holds any possessory interest in real property, and does not include a city, county, city and county, district, public corporation, or other political subdivision, public body, or public agency."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 841(c)(1), California Civil Code, definition of "landowner" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=841.)
  "“Adjoining” means contiguous to or in contact with."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 841(c)(2), California Civil Code, definition of "adjoining", treated as one source with § 841(c)(1) above, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=841.)
  Known gap: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(c)(1) and § 841(c)(2) are both subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code Section 841, and are treated here as two citations from one source, not as independent sources, not independent of one another. The statement that the statute does not define "fence" or use the phrase "good neighbor fence" describes the absence of such text in Section 841 as fetched and reviewed in full; it is not a citation to a specific provision, since there is no text to quote for an absence. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific entity or relationship in fact meets these definitions on the facts of a specific dispute.

30-DAY WRITTEN NOTICE AND SIGNATURE
NOTICE OF INTENT TO INCUR FENCE COSTS UNDER CIVIL CODE SECTION 841

Date of this notice: September 5, 2026

From: Jordan Lee, owner of the property at 123 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701
To: Morgan Casey, owner of the adjoining property at 125 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701

Fence at issue: Wood fence along the rear property line

Nature of the problem facing the shared fence: Fence panels rotted and leaning

Proposed solution: Replace with new 6-foot wood fence

Estimated construction or maintenance cost: $3,500

Proposed cost-sharing approach: Split equally, 50/50

Proposed timeline for addressing the problem: Work to begin within 45 days of this notice

Notification of presumption: Under Civil Code Section 841, adjoining landowners are presumed to share an equal benefit from a fence dividing their properties and, absent a written agreement stating otherwise, are presumed to be equally responsible for the reasonable costs described above.

Signature of Jordan Lee: _________________________ Date: _______________

This notice is dated at least 30 days before the proposed timeline stated above begins, consistent with Civil Code Section 841(b)(2)'s 30-day prior written notice requirement.
